settings.heading: What we learn at the stove
settings.text:
A grandmother teaches you to turn a flatbread by standing beside you. She can tell from a change in the sound or the way the dough lifts.

She also knows how to dry the pan and when its surface needs attention. Those habits are part of what she passes on. We started with that picture of an heirloom you know how to live with.

settings.heading: The pan in the moving box
settings.text:
After moving, Kartavya Jharwal unpacked a pan and couldn’t tell whether it would work on the new hob. Changing kitchens had separated the tool from the knowledge that made it useful.

What would the pan need to carry into its next kitchen? That question became Maison Tavo.

settings.heading: One kitchen, many tables
settings.text: In Jaipur, Kartavya managed a leased Savi property where one kitchen fed conferences, banquets and families walking in for lunch. He worked with head chefs on the standards that kept the kitchen running. A pan earned its place by being ready for the next service.

settings.heading: The work behind the menu
settings.text: At Siya, Kartavya digitised two years of handwritten kitchen registers and compared how often dishes sold with what it cost to serve them. That work informs how we think about cookware: the shape, the care routine and the parts needed for the next service all matter.

settings.heading: The house
settings.text:
Maison Tavo brings the care learned at home together with the demands of a working kitchen. The piece should feel familiar in the hand. The information that comes with it should be clear enough for the cook who picks it up next.

See how we’re building Maison Tavo

settings.heading: Our story
settings.lede: A grandmother’s tava, a pan in a moving box and the work of keeping one kitchen ready to feed a room.
